purpose: Exenatide is used to help control blood sugar levels in adults with type 2 diabetes. It is used along with diet and exercise to keep your blood sugar from getting too high. It is not used for type 1 diabetes or diabetic ketoacidosis.
how_it_works: Exenatide works by copying a natural hormone in your body called GLP-1 that helps manage blood sugar. After you eat, it tells your pancreas to release insulin, which lowers your blood sugar. It also slows down how fast food leaves your stomach and reduces the amount of sugar your liver puts into your blood, so your blood sugar stays more stable.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects are nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and upset stomach, especially when you first start the medication. You may also notice less appetite or some weight loss, which can actually be helpful. Some people get a mild reaction like redness or itching at the injection site.
warnings: There is a rare but serious risk of inflammation of the pancreas called pancreatitis — tell your doctor right away if you have severe stomach pain that does not go away. People with a personal or family history of a certain type of thyroid cancer called medullary thyroid carcinoma should not use the extended-release form Bydureon. If you also take other diabetes medications like sulfonylureas or insulin, watch for signs of low blood sugar such as shakiness, sweating, or confusion. Do not use this medication if you have severe kidney disease.
typical_dosing: Byetta (short-acting) is usually injected under the skin twice a day, within 60 minutes before your morning and evening meals, starting at 5 micrograms per dose. After about a month, your doctor may increase it to 10 micrograms twice daily. Bydureon BCise (long-acting) is injected once a week at any time of day, with or without food, at a dose of 2 mg. Never inject it into a vein or muscle — it goes just under the skin.
